open_questions: What drives the sector-dependent depth (pipeline crowding/detrending vs astrophysical blending)?
If due to a distant blended binary, its sky position is unknown; difference imaging with higher precision needed.
Sector 19 no detection suggests dilution or systematics; re-reduction with different aperture/pipeline would test.
dossier.public_summary: The dip is 2913 ppm deep and 14 days long and would be a 4.3 Earth-radius planet on the K dwarf if real. In practice its depth changes by a factor of about 30 between sectors, from no detection to depths over 6000 ppm, and the individual transits are highly inconsistent. That stability problem, together with all transits falling near one gap in the data, fits spots or blended noise much better than a planet, even though neighbours can be ruled out within one TESS pixel.

reasons.why: Depth changes by a factor ~30 between sectors, orders of magnitude larger than plausible for a planet, and sector 19 yields no detection at all despite being negative depth.

Change is statistically significant even within one light-curve product (QLP), so it is not a pipeline calibration offset but a real change in apparent depth that a planet on the target cannot produce.

reasons.why: Individual transits are highly inconsistent, with one transit essentially invisible and another ~30x deeper than the mean, indicating the signal is not a repeating, stable transit shape.
reasons.value: p_consistent=1.9904631049005647e-22 share_of_top_3=0.857 outliers depth 197 sigma -7.8 (BTJD 1826.883) and depth 6106 sigma 5.9 (BTJD 3287.74)

reasons.why: No on-target centroid to rule out a neighbour, but no nearby eclipsing binary known within 1 pixel; variability or a diluted far-field binary remains plausible given the huge depth scatter, and the planet score is well below median.
